newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-ELITE ATHLETES AND IAAF SHARE COMMON GROUND.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-ELITE ATHLETES AND IAAF SHARE COMMON GROUND.

text.p: Elite athletes and their world governing body may have reached an accord at last on the burning need to find new ways of promoting track and field.
Next May, Michael Johnson meets Donovan Bailey over 150 metres in a race to decide the world's fastest human.
"I think it's a tremendous opportunity," said Johnson shortly before the International Amateur Athletic Federation's (IAAF) annual gala dinner in Monaco last week.
"It will bring a lot of people who don't normally watch track and field to the sport. I think it's good for the sport."

News that Johnson, the Olympic 200 metres champion, is to meet Olympic 100 gold medallist Donovan Bailey in a head-to-head duel, comes at a time when the IAAF is seeking new ways to promote its sport.

IAAF president Primo Nebiolo has held informal discussions with Bernie Ecclestone, president of the Formula One Constructors' Association, to seek ways to brighten the current athletics grand prix circuit.
"We're seeking the ways to make the sport more attractive," one athletics official said. "We want new concepts to give the sport more visiblility."
The official said the IAAF council was considering reducing the number of grands prix in the 1998 season and also abolishing what is in effect a subsidy paid by the IAAF to meeting promoters.
"The president (Nebiolo) said 'We pay promoters $60,000 to stage grand prix meetings. Formula One venues pay FIA (International Motor Sport Federation)," the official said.
The official said the IAAF also wanted more head-to-head duels, rather than a constant hunt for further world records.
"We want more competition between the great athletes," he said.
The IAAF's major innovation next season will be prize money at all its world competitions, including the world indoor and outdoor championships.

Nebiolo refused to disclose the total sum at stake next season at a news conference before the IAAF gala although he did say the structure would be similar to the model used at the grand prix final. Winners at the final now earn $50,000, runners-up $30,000 and third-placed athletes $10,000.
Johnson welcomed the prize money initiative, although it has not persuaded him to run at the world indoor championships in Paris next year.
"It's a good move and a good change," he said. "It will depend on how much it is and how significant it is."

The 29-year-old American, who has been training for the past month, partly at his home in Dallas and partly in Waco, Texas, said the winner of the Olympic 100 metres was traditionally regarded as the world's fastest man.
"Every four years there's a new Olympic 100 metres champion and no-one disputes that he's the fastest man in the world. Now somebody is going to dispute it," he said.
"This is being billed as the race for the fastest man in the world. It's a head-to-head show between the two fastest men in the world."

One man who will not benefit from prize money is Carl Lewis, the nine times Olympic gold medallist who has been at the forefront of demands for more money and increased exposure for athletics since the sport turned professional in 1983.

But at the age of 35, Lewis has had enough. He will not compete for the United States at either world championships next year and will not long jump either, contenting himself with a few races over 100 metres in Europe before finally retiring.
